title: ICMP Router Discovery Messages
summary: Specifies an extension of ICMP that lets hosts on multicast or broadcast networks discover the IP addresses of neighboring routers. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: When you move into a new neighborhood, you need to find where the exits are. This helps a computer find the local gateways.

questions: what is an icmp router advertisement
subtitle: How hosts find their neighboring routers by listening for ICMP advertisements instead of reading a configuration file.

tldr.problem: Before a host can send datagrams beyond its own subnet it must know a router's address, but configuration files are a manual burden and cannot track routers coming and going, and listening to routing protocols depends on which protocols a subnet happens to use.
tldr.mechanism: Routers periodically multicast ICMP Router Advertisements carrying their addresses, a preference level and a lifetime, and hosts may send a Router Solicitation at startup to ask for an immediate advertisement.
tldr.outcome: Hosts on multicast links can learn default routers with no manual configuration and no dependence on a routing protocol. It does not choose the best router for a destination; ICMP Redirect still does that.

today: RFC 1256 is a Proposed Standard from September 1991, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few terms precisely. A router is a system that forwards IP datagrams, not counting systems with forwarding turned off or that forward only to obey source route options. A host is any system that is not a router. A multicast link is a link over which IP multicast or IP broadcast service is supported, and 'multicast' on its own means either of the two.

Two systems are neighboring if their IP addresses belong to the same subnet.
sections.eli5: A router is a computer that passes mail along between neighborhoods. A host is any other computer, and neighbors live on the same street.

sections.title: How Router Discovery Works
sections.content:
A host must discover at least one operational router on its subnet before it can send datagrams beyond it. The usual methods have drawbacks: configuration files need manual upkeep and cannot follow changes in router availability, and eavesdropping on routing protocols requires the host to recognize whichever protocols the subnet uses.

RFC 1256 defines two ICMP messages for multicast links: Router Advertisement and Router Solicitation. Each router periodically multicasts an advertisement from each multicast interface. A starting host may multicast a solicitation to get advertisements sooner. If none arrive it may retransmit a small number of times, then must stop. Routers missed because of packet loss are found later through their periodic advertisements.

These messages are not a routing protocol. They tell a host that neighboring routers exist, not which is best for a destination. A host that picks a poor first hop should get an ICMP Redirect naming a better one. Each advertised address carries a preference level, and hosts choose a default router from the addresses with the highest level. A lifetime field says how long addresses stay valid without further advertisements, so hosts forget routers that fail.

The default advertising rate is once every 7 to 10 minutes and the default lifetime is 30 minutes. These values are not enough for detecting a failed first hop, and hosts are assumed to have their own mechanism for that. They were picked to keep the load on links and hosts negligible.
sections.eli5: Routers shout out 'I am a door to the outside' every few minutes. A new computer can ask 'any doors?' to hear them sooner, and it forgets doors that stop shouting.

sections.title: The Advertisement and Solicitation Messages
sections.content:
A Router Advertisement is ICMP type 9 with code 0. After the checksum it has Num Addrs, Addr Entry Size (2 in this version, the number of 32-bit words per address) and Lifetime (maximum seconds the addresses may be considered valid). Then follow pairs of Router Address and Preference Level. The preference is a signed two's-complement value where higher means more preferable. The IP destination is the configured AdvertisementAddress or a neighboring host's address, and the time-to-live is 1 if the destination is a multicast address.

A Router Solicitation is ICMP type 10 with code 0 and a 32-bit Reserved field that is sent as 0 and ignored on reception. Its destination is the configured SolicitationAddress, and its source is an address of the sending interface or 0.
sections.eli5: The advertisement is a list of routers with a score for each. The solicitation is just a short 'is anybody there?' note.

sections.title: Router Behavior
sections.content:
A router must let management configure several variables per multicast interface. AdvertisementAddress may only be 224.0.0.1 (all-systems) or 255.255.255.255 (limited broadcast). MaxAdvertisementInterval defaults to 600 seconds and must be between 4 and 1800. MinAdvertisementInterval defaults to 0.75 times the maximum and must be at least 3 seconds. AdvertisementLifetime defaults to 3 times the maximum and may not exceed 9000 seconds. Per address, Advertise defaults to TRUE and PreferenceLevel to 0. The minimum value, hex 80000000, means the address must not be used as a default router.

Routers join the all-routers group 224.0.0.2. Advertisements are not strictly periodic: the timer is reset to a random value between the minimum and maximum interval each time, to avoid synchronizing with other routers. For the first few advertisements (up to 3) the interval is capped at 16 seconds so a new router is found quickly.

A router also answers valid solicitations, either by unicast or by multicast, after a random delay of no more than 2 seconds. When an interface stops advertising, the router is recommended (not required) to send a final advertisement with a Lifetime of zero. A router silently discards invalid solicitations, such as ones with a bad checksum or a nonzero code.
sections.eli5: Each router shouts its message at random times so that routers do not all talk at once. Right after it turns on it shouts a bit more often so it is noticed fast.

sections.title: Host Behavior
sections.content:
A host has a PerformRouterDiscovery flag (default TRUE) and a SolicitationAddress, which may only be 224.0.0.2 or 255.255.255.255. It silently discards advertisements that fail checks (bad checksum, nonzero code, Num Addrs below 1, Addr Entry Size below 2, or a message too short), and it silently discards any Router Solicitation. A host never sends a Router Advertisement.

To process an advertisement, the host ignores non-neighboring addresses. A new address is added to the default router list with a timer set to the Lifetime. An address already learned from an advertisement has its preference and timer updated. An address set by configuration is left alone and has no timer. When a timer expires, the entry is discarded. Preference levels do not change cached routes, such as ones learned through a Redirect.

After startup, interface reinitialization, a router becoming a host, or the discovery flag turning on, a host may send up to 3 solicitations, first delayed by a random time up to 1 second, then spaced 3 seconds apart. Once it receives a valid advertisement with a usable neighboring address (a preference level other than hex 80000000) it must stop soliciting.
sections.eli5: A computer writes down every router it hears about and crosses one off if it stops hearing from it. If it asks 'anyone there?' and gets an answer, it stops asking.

sections.title: Protocol Constants
sections.content: The RFC fixes these constants, all of which it says are subject to change in future revisions. Routers use MAX_INITIAL_ADVERT_INTERVAL of 16 seconds, MAX_INITIAL_ADVERTISEMENTS of 3 transmissions and MAX_RESPONSE_DELAY of 2 seconds. Hosts use MAX_SOLICITATION_DELAY of 1 second, SOLICITATION_INTERVAL of 3 seconds and MAX_SOLICITATIONS of 3 transmissions.
sections.eli5: These are the timing rules, like how long to wait and how many times you may ask before giving up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Any system on a link can pretend to be a default router. Traffic sent to such an imposter can be eavesdropped on, denied forwarding, or modified. The RFC notes that on most links where the protocol is expected to run, eavesdropping is already possible, and ARP offers a similar chance for denial and modification. Where the threat is unacceptable, host configuration variables can disable dynamic router discovery.

Because the advertisement format can carry extra information compatibly, digital signatures or other authentication could later be added. The RFC marks this as for further study.
sections.eli5: A sneaky computer could pretend to be a router and trick others into sending their mail through it. Computers can be told not to listen to such signs.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: One's complement checksum of the ICMP message.

fields.name: Num Addrs
fields.desc: Number of router addresses in the message.

fields.name: Lifetime
fields.desc: Maximum seconds the addresses are valid.

fields.name: Router Address[1]
fields.desc: Sending router's IP address on this interface.

fields.name: Preference Level[1]
fields.desc: Signed value; higher is more preferable.
